statement: Both inverse-limit assertions for a closed subset of a regular Hausdorff space, including their universal properties on geometric morphisms.
source_statement_latex: \label{A1.1} Suppose that $Z$ is a regular Hausdorff space and $Y\subset Z$ is closed. The inverse limit in $\Topos$ of the open subtopoi $\Sh(N)\subset\Sh(Z)$, for $N$ ranging over all neighborhoods of $Y$, is $\Sh(Y)$. The analogous limit of $\Sh(N\setminus Y)$ is the empty topos. Thus taking this limit before gluing discards precisely the punctured-neighborhood information.

statement: The locally finite closed-family cover, degree-0/1/2 ordinary-topos bicolimit, synchronized 2-Pro bicolimit, finite-index subset presentation, and prohibition on an infinite product interchange.
source_statement_latex: \label{A1.2} For every tuple $\alpha=(N_i)_{i\in I}$ of open neighborhoods $N_i\supset X_i$ in $X$, put \[ W_i^\alpha=N_i\setminus R_i^{\mathrm{ord}},\qquad C_q^\alpha=\Sh\left(\coprod_{(i_0,\ldots,i_q)\in I^{q+1}} W_{i_0}^\alpha\cap\cdots\cap W_{i_q}^\alpha\right). \tag{A.1.4}\label{eq:tubecech} \] The $W_i^\alpha$ form an open cover of $X$. Their augmented Cech diagram has the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item For every fixed $\alpha$, its truncation in degrees $0,1,2$ has $\Sh(X)$ as its bicolimit in $\Topos$. \item Regard each $C_q=(C_q^\alpha)_\alpha$ as a \emph{single synchronized pro-object}. Then \[ \mathop{\mathrm{bicolim}}_{[q]\in\Delta_{\leq2}^{\mathrm{op}}}C_q \simeq c\Sh(X) \quad\text{in }2\Pro(\Topos). \tag{A.1.5}\label{eq:procech} \] \item If $I$ is finite, one can equivalently use the individual nonempty intersections $W_A=(\Sh(\bigcap_{i\in A}W_i^\alpha))_\alpha$ for $1\leq |A|\leq3$, with all their face inclusions. For infinite $I$, the synchronized pro-coproducts in (\ref{eq:tubecech}) are part of the assertion; no interchange of an infinite product and a filtered colimit is asserted. \end{enumerate} No Thom--Mather, Whitney, or homotopy-link assumption is needed. Such assumptions are needed for geometric models and homotopy replacements of the intersections, not for this descent theorem.

statement: Exact membership-groupoid criterion for any small inclusion diagram of opens on a T1 space; the resulting permitted-deletion minimality test.
source_statement_latex: \label{A1.5} Let $X$ be a $T_1$ space, $C$ a small category, and $D:C\to\operatorname{Open}(X)$ a diagram of open subsets and inclusions. For $x\in X$, let $C_x$ be the full subcategory on the objects $c$ with $x\in D(c)$. The canonical cocone has $\Sh(X)$ as its bicolimit if and only if the groupoid obtained by inverting every arrow of $C_x$ is equivalent to the terminal groupoid, for every $x$. Equivalently, each $|N(C_x)|$ is nonempty, connected, and simply connected. This gives an exact test for any proposed deletion of objects or arrows from a specified honest-open gluing diagram. An inclusion-minimal subdiagram is precisely one satisfying this test for which every further permitted deletion fails the test at some point.

Equivalently, for every closed $F'\subset Z'$ disjoint from $f^{-1}Y$, there is an open $N\supset Y$ with $f^{-1}N\cap F'=\varnothing$. This holds for every closed continuous map $f$, in particular for proper maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces. No local-immersion hypothesis is necessary.

statement: Natural germ comparison; exact Hom-set criterion over a fixed pair; necessity of an isomorphism after all local restrictions; sufficient conical local-system stability.
source_statement_latex: Suppose in addition that $N\subset X$ is an open neighbourhood of $Y$ with a retraction $r:N\to Y$, and write $N^*=N\setminus Y$ and $p=r|_{N^*}:N^*\to Y$. For $L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U)$ there is a natural germ comparison \[ \theta_L:p_*(L|_{N^*})\longrightarrow i^{-1}j_*L. \tag{B1.3} \] Indeed a section over $p^{-1}W$ gives a germ along the open subset $W\subset Y$ by using the neighbourhood $r^{-1}W$. If every $\theta_L$ is an isomorphism, then \[ \mathcal F\simeq \{(L,E,\varphi):L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U),\ E\in\operatorname{Loc}(Y),\ \varphi:p^{-1}E\longrightarrow L|_{N^*}\}. \tag{B1.4} \] More generally, without assuming (B1.3) to be an isomorphism, the precise necessary and sufficient condition for this functor of systems to be an equivalence over the fixed pair $(L,E)$ is that \[ \operatorname{Hom}_Y(E,p_*(L|_{N^*}))\longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_Y(E,i^{-1}j_*L) \tag{B1.5} \] be bijective. Requiring the description after restriction to every open subset of $Y$, and for every locally constant $E$, makes the isomorphism condition on (B1.3) necessary as well as sufficient.

statement: Equivariant gluing into inertia fixed points, quotient inertia via the homotopy exact sequence, asphericity consequence, and groupoid qualification for disconnected fibers.
source_statement_latex: In the connected case let $D=\pi_1(N^*)$, $B=\pi_1(Y)$ and $G=\pi_1(U)$, with homomorphisms $p_*:D\to B$ and $i_*:D\to G$. Assume $p_*$ is onto and put $I=\ker p_*$. Then (18) of 151/036 is equivalent to the $B$-equivariant map \[ E\longrightarrow (i_*^*L)^I. \tag{B1.6} \] Indeed a $D$-equivariant map from a $D$-set on which $I$ acts trivially has image in the $I$-fixed points, and the induced action on those fixed points factors through $D/I=B$. Conversely such a $B$-map is $D$-equivariant. If $p$ is a fibration with connected fibre $K$, its homotopy exact sequence gives \[ \pi_2(Y)\longrightarrow\pi_1(K)\longrightarrow D \longrightarrow B\longrightarrow1. \tag{B1.7} \] Thus $I$ is the quotient of $\pi_1(K)$ by the image of the connecting homomorphism, and it equals $\pi_1(K)$ only when that homomorphism is zero. This independently rechecks R4, SA10-C3-04. If $Y$ and $K$ are aspherical, the same long exact sequence gives $\pi_q(N^*)=0$ for $q\geq2$. Disconnected fibres are handled by the groupoid formulation; surjectivity of $D\to B$ must not then be silently asserted.

statement: Exact equivalence criterion for local-system extension and uniform gluing-morphism extension on synchronized neighborhood categories.
source_statement_latex: We give a criterion that does not assume a chosen retraction or a stationary representative. Let $\mathcal N_Y$ be the filtered ordered set of open neighbourhoods of $Y$, with arrows given by shrinking. Form the filtered bicategorical colimits in categories \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal T&=\operatorname*{2colim}_{N\in\mathcal N_Y} \operatorname{Loc}(N),\\ \mathcal T^*&=\operatorname*{2colim}_{N\in\mathcal N_Y} \operatorname{Loc}(N\setminus Y). \end{aligned} \tag{B1.8} \] Their objects and arrows have representatives on one neighbourhood; two representatives agree if they agree after a common shrinking. There are restriction functors $r:\mathcal T\to\operatorname{Loc}(Y)$, $a:\mathcal T\to\mathcal T^*$, and $b:\operatorname{Loc}(U)\to\mathcal T^*$. For $E\in\mathcal T$ and $L\in\operatorname{Loc}(U)$, restriction of a representative morphism to germs along $Y$ defines \[ \mu_{E,L}:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T^*}(aE,bL) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{Y}(rE,i^{-1}j_*L). \tag{B1.9} \] The natural functor from systems $(L,E,\varphi:aE\to bL)$ to $\mathcal F$ is an equivalence, compatible with restriction to $U$ and $Y$, if and only if both of the following conditions hold: $r$ is an equivalence, and every map (B1.9) is bijective. These are respectively an extension condition for local systems and a uniform extension condition for their gluing morphisms. For a cofinal system of actual tube retractions, B1.2 supplies sufficient geometric hypotheses for both conditions.

statement: A forward-tame closed subset of a metric space gives a homotopy-pushout decomposition by the subset, complement, and homotopy link, while a normal-fibration condition alone does not supply tameness and ordinary quotient cylinders must be distinguished from controlled ones.
source_statement_latex: For a metric space $X$ and a closed subset $Y$, put \[ H=\operatorname{holink}(X,Y) =\{\gamma:[0,1]\to X:\gamma(0)\in Y, \ \gamma(t)\notin Y\ (t>0)\}. \] The maps $e_0:H\to Y$ and $e_1:H\to U$ are endpoint evaluations. If $Y$ is forward tame in $X$, then the ordinary homotopy types satisfy \[ X\simeq Y\mathbin{\cup^h}_{H}U. \tag{B2.4} \] Quinn proves a controlled strict relative version in \cite[Lemma 2.4(2)]{Quinn1988}, using his controlled holink and mapping-cylinder convention. We give a separate proof of (B2.4) that does not identify that cylinder topology with the ordinary quotient-cylinder topology. Let $N$ range over the open neighborhoods of $Y$. The numerable open cover $X=N\cup U$ gives, naturally in $N$, the homotopy-pushout equivalence $N\cup^h_{N\setminus Y}U\simeq X$. A fixed tame deformation gives an equivalence $\{N\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}Y$ in prospaces: for any target neighborhood $N$, shrink to the points whose entire deformation lies in $N$. The same fixed deformation and the explicit endpoint-preserving path homotopy of C4.02 give $\{N\setminus Y\}_N\simeq\operatorname{const}H$. Those formulas need only tameness of this pair; the fibration part of the HSS definition is not used. The comparison uses the natural zigzag through paths wholly contained in $N$, so its endpoint maps and the homotopy between the two maps to $X$ are the original ones. The finite span colimit in $\operatorname{Pro}(\mathcal S)$ is computed on these synchronized levels, because filtered colimits of spaces commute with finite simplicial limits. Replacing the two pro-germs by their constant equivalents therefore gives $\operatorname{const}X\simeq \operatorname{const}(Y\cup^h_HU)$. The constant embedding is fully faithful, proving (B2.4). In the usual quotient double-cylinder model, the associated map to $X$ is induced by the continuous path evaluation $H\times[0,1]\to X$. Quinn's Definition 3.1 adds, for each incident pair of strata, that $e_0$ is a fibration. That is the precise normal-fibration analogue of 151/032, once a deleted tube has been compared with the holink. It is not the whole definition: forward tameness remains a separate hypothesis. The fibration condition alone does not imply tameness. For the Hawaiian earring with $Y$ its common point, $e_0$ is a fibration because its target is a point. But $Y$ is not tame: a neighbourhood deformation into $Y$ would null-homotope every sufficiently small circle in $X$, while retraction of $X$ onto any one of those circles shows its fundamental loop is nonzero. Consequently L2 must be read with this additional tameness and comparison data, and its unrestricted topos-colimit conclusion must be replaced by B2.1. The shape theorem itself needs neither condition.

statement: The plane and point-stratified sphere constructible-sheaf categories have contractible functor-topos shapes, while the sphere's genuine tube span recovers S2.
source_statement_latex: For $(\mathbb C,\{0\})$, B1.4 identifies a constructible sheaf with a set $E$, a $\mathbb Z$-set $M$, and a map $E\to M^{\mathbb Z}$. Equivalently it is a covariant set-valued functor on the category with objects $p,q$, automorphism group $\mathbb Z$ at $q$, and a unique map $p\to q$. The object $p$ is initial; hence the classifying space of this category, and the shape of its functor topos, is contractible. This agrees with $\mathbb C$. For $(S^2,\{p\})$, the complementary plane is contractible. The same description reduces to a single map of sets $E\to M$. The corresponding arrow category also has contractible classifying space. Nevertheless the genuine tube span has shapes \[ *\longleftarrow S^1\longrightarrow *, \] whose homotopy pushout is $\Sigma S^1\simeq S^2$. Thus the ordinary constructible-sheaf topos does not retain the sphere's higher homotopy type. This proves the assertions SA10-C3-05 and SA10-C3-06 without identifying that functor topos with the required higher gluing.

statement: For a paracompact locally singular-shape conically stratified space with ascending-chain-condition poset, constructible n-truncated sheaves are functors from its exit infinity-category and depend exactly on the n-truncated mapping spaces, with genuine stratum regularity required.
source_statement_latex: Assume that $X$ is paracompact, locally of singular shape, and conically stratified by a poset $P$ satisfying the ascending chain condition. These hypotheses hold, for example, for a finite-dimensional, paracompact Hausdorff topologically stratified space with the compact conical charts used in \cite[Definition 3.1]{Treumann2009}. Write $\operatorname{Exit}(X)=\operatorname{Sing}_P(X)$. For every integer $n\geq0$ there are equivalences \[ \begin{split} \operatorname{Cons}_{\leq n}(X) &\simeq \operatorname{Fun}(\operatorname{Exit}(X),\mathcal S_{\leq n})\\ &\simeq \operatorname{Fun}(h_{n+1}\operatorname{Exit}(X), \mathcal S_{\leq n}). \end{split} \tag{B3.1} \] Here the left side consists of constructible $n$-truncated sheaves of spaces, and $h_{n+1}$ retains the objects and the $n$-truncations of all mapping spaces, with their coherent compositions. The regularity hypotheses on the strata are substantive. If ``conical'' only means a local product with a cone, allowing an arbitrary unstratified base, every one-stratum space is conical. The Cantor-space example after B1.3 then refutes the unqualified claim already at $n=0$, and also at every higher level by regarding sets as discrete spaces. For the usual finite Thom--Mather, Whitney, or conically smooth spaces with manifold strata, the hypotheses used here hold. Disconnected and empty strata cause no change: the statement is componentwise and an empty stratum contributes no objects.

statement: Constructible stacks in groupoids use the exit two-category and retain link fundamental groups that set-valued constructible sheaves discard, while banded gerbes form the narrower subproblem whose honest open-overlap gluing arrows are equivalences.
source_statement_latex: At $n=1$, (B3.1) is the equivalence between constructible stacks in groupoids and homotopy-coherent $2$-functors from the exit-path $2$-category to groupoids. It is also the restriction of \cite[Theorem 7.14]{Treumann2009} from category-valued to groupoid-valued stacks: the value at each object is the stalk category, so the condition that these values are groupoids is preserved in both directions. His Theorem 7.13 proves compatibility with open-cover descent. The set-valued level, by contrast, is $n=0$: it retains $\pi_0$ of each exit mapping space. Thus L3's phrase ``truncated at $\pi_1$ of the links'' is one level too high if it means that link $\pi_1$ survives as automorphisms of exiting arrows. Those automorphisms first appear in the stack level. For $(S^2,\{p\})$, the two-stratum exit category can be represented by two objects and cross mapping space $S^1$: the open stratum is contractible, and its attaching holink has the homotopy type of $S^1$. Taking $\pi_0$ makes a single arrow, while the fundamental groupoid of that mapping space retains $\mathbb Z$. This is exactly the difference seen by the gerbes. One should also distinguish two uses of gluing. A general constructible stack is a closed--open system (B3.2), with a possibly noninvertible functor to nearby data. An $A$-banded gerbe is locally equivalent to $BA$ at every point of $X$. Its gluing over an honest open tube and $U$ uses an \emph{equivalence} on their overlap, as in 151/042. These gerbes form a subproblem of the constructible-stack theorem; arbitrary constructible stacks are not all gerbes.

statement: Complete strict-chain exit-space assembly; when every stratum and total incident-pair space is a 1-type, all coherent groupoids determine the full homotopy type.
source_statement_latex: Let $X\to P$ satisfy the hypotheses of B3.1, and put $\mathcal E=\operatorname{Exit}(X)$. For every nonempty strict chain $\sigma=(p_0<\cdots<p_m)$ in $P$, define \[ D(\sigma)=\operatorname{Map}_{/P}(\sigma,\mathcal E). \tag{B4.3} \] This is a space: a natural transformation over the fixed chain has components inside strata, hence all its components are equivalences. Restriction along subchains defines a homotopy-coherent functor $D:\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal S$. Without any asphericity assumption, the complete assembly formula is \[ \operatorname{Sing}(X)\simeq \operatorname*{colim}_{\sigma\in\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}} D(\sigma). \tag{B4.3a} \] Assume that every stratum $D(p)$ and every total incidence link $D(p<q)$ is a $1$-type. Then the groupoids \[ G_\sigma=\Pi_1D(\sigma), \qquad G:\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gpd}, \tag{B4.4} \] with \emph{all} restriction functors and their coherent comparison isomorphisms determine the full homotopy type: \[ \operatorname{Sing}(X)\simeq \operatorname*{colim}_{\sigma\in\operatorname{sd}(P)^{\mathrm{op}}} BG_\sigma. \tag{B4.5} \] The colimit in (B4.5) is taken in spaces, not in ordinary groupoids. The incidence-link hypothesis holds when the local homotopy links are aspherical and their source maps are fibrations over aspherical strata. In geometric applications, ``all links'' must mean all incident pairs, not merely adjacent pairs or a union of different link strata.

statement: All stated incomparability/strictness relations for ordinary and symmetric flatness, forest conditions and Verdier hypercovers, including both exact counterexamples and the linear-order classification over sets.
source_statement_latex: \label{b5.5.-flatness-forest-comparisons-and-verdier-hypercovers} \textbf{Status: Refuted for the proposed ``strictly between'' description.} A hypercover condition agreeing with Verdier's cannot in general lie between the manuscript's forest conditions and flatness. For \(A=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\), the ordinary Cech nerve \(U_n=\{0,1\}^{n+1}\) of a cover of a point is a hypercover, and its realization is the contractible nerve of the indiscrete groupoid on two objects. Yet Hyp \(2'\) fails. Take in \(\Delta\) the span \([0]\leftarrow[1]\to[2]\), with the first map constant and the second selecting endpoints 0,2. The corresponding fiber product contains \((0,(0,1,0))\). A cocone must have a monotone map \([2]\to[m]\) with equal endpoint values, hence a constant map. Every tuple lifted from a completing cone is therefore constant in those three positions. The displayed element has no lift. In particular full (Hyp) fails as well. Conversely, \(\Delta[1]\) is a flat functor on \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\): its extension is evaluation at \([1]\). It is not a hypercover of a point, because its degree-one matching map omits the ordered pair of vertices \((1,0)\). Thus even flatness and Verdier's condition are incomparable for ordinary simplicial indexing. The failure of ``between'' persists for symmetric indexing. Put \(U(S)=\operatorname{Cont}(\Delta(S),\mathbf R)\), with maps by affine precomposition. Every continuous boundary map to \(\mathbf R\) extends to the simplex by coning from the barycenter and interpolating to zero; compactness gives continuity at the barycenter. Hence the ordinary simplicial restriction is a hypercover of a point. For the finite-set span \(1\leftarrow2\to3\), with the right map selecting vertices 0,2, take zero on \(\Delta^0\) and \[b(t_0,t_1,t_2)=t_1(t_0-t_2).\] They agree on edge 02. Any amalgamating finite-set map identifies vertices 0,2, so its affine map takes \((1/2,1/2,0)\) and \((0,1/2,1/2)\) to the same point. A lifted function must have equal values there; \(b\) has values \(1/4,-1/4\). Thus Hyp \(2'\) fails. Exact rational computation checks this obstruction on 30 amalgams; the argument proves it for every target cardinality. There is nevertheless a one-way implication specific to symmetric indexing: full (Hyp) implies the hypercover condition. By B5.4 its system is \(U(S)=E^S\) with \(E\to1\) epic. The simplicial restriction is the Cech nerve of this epimorphism; every positive matching map is an isomorphism. The symmetric continuous-simplex example just given proves the converse false. Thus ordinary flatness and hypercovers are incomparable, whereas symmetric flatness is strictly stronger than hypercovers; in either case hypercovers need not satisfy the forest conditions. Over sets there is also an explicit ordinary-index classification: flat functors \(\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}\) are precisely nerves of nonempty linear orders. Indeed a flat functor is a filtered colimit of the covariant representables \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}}([n],-)=\Delta[n]\). A filtered colimit of finite ordinals and monotone maps is a linear order: comparisons and antisymmetry are witnessed at a common stage. Nerves commute with filtered colimits, since finite strings use finite limits of sets. Conversely a linear order is the filtered union of its nonempty finite suborders. The filtered-colimit characterization follows from the cofiltered element-category argument in B5.4. \(\square\) This corrects \path{study/readings/151_001-017_INTEGRATION.md} lines 61--68, 78--83, and \path{study/readings/151_001-017.md} lines 303--309. The assertion that the comparison scheme lies strictly between forest conditions and flatness is not a valid requirement for the desired Verdier comparison.

statement: Exact all-K shape mapping test; H_phi=1 sufficient; full ordinary Hyp gives this before and after hypercompletion; forest conditions do not and full Hyp is unnecessary.
source_statement_latex: \label{b5.6.-exact-general-homotopy-colimit-criterion} \textbf{Status: Proved under the stated interpretation.} Let \(\mathscr X\) denote either the associated 1-localic infinity-topos or its hypercompletion; fix this choice in each formula. Regard \(U_a\) as 0-truncated objects of \(\mathscr X\). Form \[B_\varphi{}_n=\coprod_{a_0\to\cdots\to a_n}U_{a_0},\qquad H_\varphi=|B_\varphi|=\operatorname{colim}_{a\in A}U_a.\] The first face uses \(U_{a_0}\to U_{a_1}\), inner faces compose arrows, the last face drops the last arrow, and degeneracies insert identities. The augmentation \(\epsilon:H_\varphi\to1\) is the terminal comparison of the derived colimit extension \(\mathbf L\varphi_!:\mathcal P(A)\to\mathscr X\), since \(1_{\mathcal P(A)}=\operatorname{colim}_{a\in A}y(a)\). There is a canonical map \[\operatorname{colim}_{a\in A}\Pi_\infty(\mathscr X/U_a)\longrightarrow\Pi_\infty(\mathscr X).\tag{B5.6.1}\] It is an equivalence of pro-spaces if and only if for every space \(K\) the canonical map \[\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr X}(1,\Delta K)\longrightarrow \lim_{a\in A^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathscr X}(U_a,\Delta K)\tag{B5.6.2}\] is an equivalence. It suffices that \(\epsilon\) be an equivalence. Full ordinary (Hyp) suffices for this stronger assertion even before hypercompletion; the forest conditions do not, by B5.2. Full (Hyp) is not necessary, by B5.5.

statement: Verdier matching maps, infinity-connected realization and hypercomplete terminality; exact boundary-representable comparison in the specified ordinary/symmetric degrees.
source_statement_latex: \label{b5.7.-verdier-matching-as-comparisons-of-representables} \textbf{Status: Known, with the precise derivation given.} Define \[M_nU=\lim_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq\{0,\ldots,n\}}U_{|S|-1},\qquad M_0U=1,\] with face restriction arrows. The conditions \(U_n\to M_nU\) epic for all \(n\ge0\) are the hypercover conditions. The realization is infinity-connected in \(\mathcal X_\infty\) and terminal after hypercompletion. This is HTT Definition 6.5.3.2, Lemma 6.5.3.11 and Theorem 6.5.3.12 \cite{B56HTT} (or DHI Definition 4.2 and Proposition 3.2). For \(A=\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\) and \(n\ge2\), the limit in \(\widehat A\) of the representables of all proper nonempty faces of \([n]\) is \(y[n]\). Consequently its comparison \(c_F\) is precisely \(U_n\to M_nU\). Degrees zero and one must be added separately. For \(A=\mathsf F^{\mathrm{op}}\) the same statement holds for all \(n\ge1\), so all positive-degree matching conditions are the corresponding boundary comparisons, with degree zero \(U(1)\to1\).

statement: Exact local finite-boundary filling after subdivision criterion for H_phi=1 in the hypercomplete infinity-topos.
source_statement_latex: \label{b5.10.-an-explicit-all-index-local-filling-criterion} \textbf{Status: Known criterion, derived here in the required form.} The exact stronger condition \(H_\varphi=1\) in the hypercomplete infinity-topos has an explicit test using the original \(U_a\), finite limits, coproducts and a sequential colimit. It does not require one to guess boundary objects in the arbitrary category \(A\). Let \(N=B_\varphi\) be the simplicial replacement from B5.6; equivalently it is the nerve of the internal element category, whose objects are \(\coprod_aU_a\) and whose arrow object is \(\coprod_{a\to b}U_a\). For a finite simplicial set \(K\), let \([K,N]\) be the object of simplicial maps, expressed as a finite limit using the nondegenerate simplices of \(K\). Put \[R_n=\operatorname*{colim}_{r\ge0}[\operatorname{Sd}^{r}\Delta^n,N],\] with the transition maps induced by the standard last-vertex subdivision maps. Here colimits and finite limits are in \(\mathcal X\), and \(\operatorname{Sd}\) is barycentric subdivision. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.} \tightlist \item \(H_\varphi\to1\) is an equivalence after hypercompletion. \item The simplicial replacement \(N\to1\) is a local weak equivalence. \item For every \(n\ge0\), the following explicit map is an epimorphism in \(\mathcal X\): \end{enumerate} \[\operatorname*{colim}_{r\ge0}[\operatorname{Sd}^{r}\Delta^n,N] \longrightarrow \operatorname*{colim}_{r\ge0}[\operatorname{Sd}^{r}\partial\Delta^n,N].\tag{B5.10.1}\] For \(n=0\) the right side is terminal. Since filtered colimits commute with finite limits in a Grothendieck topos, the right side is precisely \(M_nR\). Thus (3) is an ordinary epimorphic matching-map scheme on the explicitly derived simplicial object \(R\). It says that every finite boundary admits a filling locally after sufficiently many subdivisions. The required subdivision number may vary over the covering family; no assertion of algorithmic decidability is made.

statement: The four manuscript relations remain incomplete even after both displayed global invariance families, in every degree.

statement: All explicit substitution words and translated Grandis relations give a complete presentation on the old generators in every positive arity.
source_statement_latex: \label{b6.2.-a-complete-replacement-is-available-in-the-primary-literature} \textbf{Status: Known, with a direct translation to the manuscript generators.} Grandis, \emph{Finite sets and symmetric simplicial sets}, §3 and Theorem 4.2 \cite{B56Grandis2001}, gives a complete presentation of finite cardinals by all elementary cofaces, codegeneracies and adjacent transpositions, subject to the cosimplicial, symmetric-group and mixed interchange relations. His §5 restricts the presentation to nonempty finite cardinals. Thus a complete corrected presentation is obtained by adding all these translated relations to the manuscript generators. Here are explicit substitution words, including their arities. Write \(c_i^{(m)}=(i\ i+1\ \cdots\ m)\in\mathfrak S_m\), with \(c_m^{(m)}=1\). For the coface \(d_i^{(n)}:n\to n+1\) omitting \(i\), and the codegeneracy \(e_i^{(n)}:n+1\to n\) identifying \(i,i+1\), set \[ d_i^{(n)}=c_i^{(n+1)}\delta_n\quad(1\le i\le n+1),\qquad e_i^{(n)}=c_i^{(n)}K_n\bigl(c_i^{(n+1)}\bigr)^{-2} \quad(1\le i\le n). \tag{B6.2.1} \] Adjacent transpositions are \(s_i=(i\ i+1)\), already present in the symmetric groups. The first word fixes positions before \(i\) and moves every later old position one step to the right. In the second word, the source permutation fixes \(k<i\), sends \(i,i+1\) to \(n,n+1\), and sends \(k>i+1\) to \(k-2\); \(K_n\) merges the last two, and the output cycle puts the merged value back in position \(i\). Thus these are exactly the indicated finite-set maps. Crucially, the last words recover the old generators literally: \(d_{n+1}^{(n)}=\delta_n\) and \(e_n^{(n)}=K_n\). For a completely explicit enlarged relation scheme, use (B6.2.1) in all the following formulas, whenever their arities are positive and well typed; dimension superscripts are suppressed: \[ d_i d_j=d_{j+1}d_i\ (i\le j),\qquad e_j e_i=e_i e_{j+1}\ (i\le j), \] \[ e_jd_i= \begin{cases} d_i e_{j-1},&i<j,\\ 1,&i=j\text{ or }i=j+1,\\ d_{i-1}e_j,&i>j+1; \end{cases} \] \[ s_i^2=1,\quad s_i s_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1},\quad s_i s_j=s_j s_i\ (i<j-1), \] \[ \begin{array}{lll} s_i d_j=d_j s_i &(i<j-1),&s_i e_j=e_j s_i\quad(i<j-1),\\ s_i d_i=d_{i+1},&&s_i e_i=e_{i+1}s_i s_{i+1},\\ s_i d_j=d_j s_{i-1}&(i>j),&s_i e_j=e_j s_{i+1}\quad(i>j), \end{array} \qquad e_i s_i=e_i. \tag{B6.2.2} \] These are Grandis's (3), (10), (12), (13), with indices shifted from zero-based to one-based notation. The omitted mixed cases follow by \(s_i^2=1\), exactly as in Grandis. The group equations are redundant if the complete groups \(\mathfrak S_n\) and their multiplication laws are retained as the manuscript prescribes. We verify carefully that no unspoken defining equations are missing. Let \(P\) be Grandis's presented category on positive cardinals and let \(Q\) be the category on the manuscript generators with their group laws, the valid manuscript equations, and all of (B6.2.2) after the substitutions (B6.2.1). Substitution defines a functor \(F:P\to Q\), because every defining relation of \(P\) has explicitly been imposed in \(Q\). This functor is surjective on every hom-set: its image contains \(\delta_n\) and \(K_n\) literally and contains all adjacent transpositions, which generate each of the already imposed symmetric groups. The finite-set interpretation gives \(G:Q\to\mathsf F\), because every imposed relation holds for these functions. The composite \(GF\) is the standard interpretation of Grandis's generators and is an isomorphism by Theorem 4.2 and §5. For faithfulness of \(G\), choose lifts \(u,v\) in \(P\) of two parallel arrows of \(Q\). Equality of their \(G\)-images gives \(GF(u)=GF(v)\), hence \(u=v\), and hence equality of the arrows in \(Q\). Fullness follows from the same composite. Thus \(Q\cong\mathsf F\), with exactly the requested old generators. This proof does not assume that generator substitutions are inverses without checking their defining equations. The auxiliary script \texttt{check\_B6\_translation.py} verifies all 168 coface and codegeneracy words for \(1\le n\le12\); the explicit coordinate argument above proves the formulas in every arity. We make no minimality claim for this enlarged relation list. Exact locator: Grandis, \emph{Theory and Applications of Categories} \textbf{8} (2001), no. 8, 244--252; §3, printed pp.~247--248; Theorem 4.2, p.~249; §5, p.~250. The full primary PDF was opened and downloaded. No novelty is claimed for this replacement.

statement: The corrected low-degree relation list with final subscript one presents the opposite category of sets of cardinality at most three, whereas the alternative final subscript three or the uncorrected earlier relation gives a false presentation, with the last original mark remaining paleographically unresolved.
source_statement_latex: \label{b6.3.-the-corrected-low-degree-presentation-is-complete} \textbf{Status: Proved for the corrected 151/005 reading; refuted for the explicitly identified alternatives.} The final relations of 151/005 present the full subcategory \(\mathsf F_{\le3}^{\mathrm{op}}\), provided the last subscript is \(1\). statement: Complete simultaneous-cylinder diagram, including prefix maps, has colimit canonically homeomorphic to strict-nerve realization; recursive conical model reconstructs the space.

statement: Translation between the precise smooth iterated boundary-fibration system and the cited compact/noncompact resolution object theorems, with both control identities and radial data retained.

statement: The literal recursive conical datum preserving all earlier boundaries always unzips to a precylindrical structure, which is a manifold with its specified corners exactly when every full local face intersection is a manifold and all collar transitions have the chosen TOP, PL, or smooth regularity.

For the finite recursive conical data actually defined on 150/035--036, retaining the boundaries always gives a precylindrical structure in the manuscript's collar sense. This assertion does not require source fibrancy. The induction is explicit in the original /036, visually checked: after cutting the minimal strata, (22) contains the old collared boundaries together with every new link boundary, as a mutually transverse family transverse to the remaining strata; the next conical datum is required on this entire system. Here is the inductive verification. A cut replaces each selected cone direction by its radius interval and retains its zero-radius boundary. Conical transversality to an old boundary says in coordinates that this cut is a product with the old collar coordinate; hence each old collar restricts to the cut piece and commutes with the new collar. Distinct simultaneously cut minimal strata are disjoint, so their new faces are disjoint. By the recursive requirement the next cuts are products with all the retained coordinates. This proves the transverse-collar axioms at every stage and on every removed base piece \(\Sigma_i\). Two incoming labels that are incomparable cannot meet: their original closed strata intersect only in lower strata, and, after those lower strata have been cut, a common positive-radius link point would give a point of both original strata outside that lower intersection. Thus all nonempty face intersections have flag labels. Their subface intervals are the Boolean intervals proved in C3.02. The intersection of two such closed faces is the face for the union of their labels when that union is an admissible flag, and is empty otherwise; local incidence branches are retained separately. Including the full pieces and deleting empty faces verifies the finite closed-cover and intersection axioms (14). This proves precylindricity for each cut-open piece and hence for the maximal pieces comprising the full unzip of the literal recursive \S{}8 datum. For any of TOP, PL, or smooth, fix a finite precylindrical structure with the stated compatible collars and incidence branches. At a point \(x\), let \(F_x^\circ\) be the open face obtained by intersecting precisely the boundary germs through \(x\), and deleting all smaller faces. Let \(k(x)\) be the number of those independent germs. The collar axioms provide a germ \[ (X,x)\cong (F_x^\circ,x)\times([0,\infty)^{k(x)},0) \] respecting each specified face. The resulting space is a manifold with these corners in the chosen category if and only if every \(F_x^\circ\) is a manifold in that category and the collar transition maps have that regularity. Its dimension is locally constant; for a single prescribed dimension \(n\), also require \(\dim F_x^\circ+k(x)=n\) for every point. Empty outputs satisfy the convention vacuously. Indeed, a local manifold chart on \(F_x^\circ\), followed by the collar product, is exactly an orthant chart of dimension \(\dim F_x^\circ+k(x)\). Conversely a corner chart preserving all the prescribed faces restricts on their full intersection to a manifold chart on \(F_x^\circ\). Both implications are local; compatibility gives an atlas. The same endpoint map is used at all levels, so these are compatible pro maps, not unrelated levelwise equivalences. This proves (51). If \(Z\) is a locally closed union of strata containing \(S_i\), the homotopy on \(W_U\cap Z\) stays in \(Z\), including its endpoint, proving both arrows of (56). \textbf{Flag germs.} Let \(d=(i_0<\cdots<i_n=j)\), and fix target neighborhoods \(U_{i_k}\) for every flag entry. First shrink \(N_j\) so that its whole fixed homotopy stays in \(U_j\). First choose cofinal representatives for which every upper-band neighbourhood \(U_l\) lies in the open upper union \(X_L^*\subset X'\). Their union is then exactly \(X_L^*\). Consequently the union of the pairwise cover pieces \(U_j\cap U_l\) is exactly \(V_J\cap X_L^*=V_J^L\) at that stage. All flags in \(D\) have maximum in \(L\), so their intersections are actual opens of this union. Thus no homotopy invariance of arbitrary sheaf cohomology is being invoked. Choose these representatives for the finite open cover and a flabby resolution of \(F\). Form the double complex whose degree \((p,q)\) is the product of \(\Gamma(V_{d_p},\mathcal I^q)\) over chains \(d_0\subset\cdots\subset d_p\), with the usual alternating restriction differential horizontally. Its horizontal augmentation computes sections on the union. Exactness can be checked locally inside a covering piece: adjoining that piece to an intersection gives the common refinement and contracts the augmented \v{C}ech complex; empty intersections contribute zero. More precisely use the augmented complex of sheaves obtained by direct image from the open intersections. On a covering open set, contraction is by adjoining its flag; a nonflag union has empty intersection and contributes zero. This local contraction proves exactness without identifying the stalk of an open direct image outside its open set with zero. With a flabby resolution, all the open direct images are flabby. Flabbiness makes all restriction terms acyclic for sections, so the total complex computes sheaf cohomology on the union. Taking vertical cohomology first yields the derived-limit complex of the coefficient diagram \(d\mapsto H^q(V_d,F)\), proving the displayed \(E_2\)-page. Taking filtered colimits over representative neighborhoods is exact in abelian groups and commutes with the finite products here. Finally \(D\) has bounded chain length, so the horizontal filtration is finite; there is no convergence or product-completion ambiguity. Empty \(D\) gives the empty union and zero groups.

statement: General Quinn HSS need not admit actual conical mapping-cylinder collars, via the compact shrinking hedgehog.
source_statement_latex: \label{c4.04-refuted-hss-alone-gives-conical-collars} Quinn's example \cite[p.452]{Quinn1988} is the shrinking hedgehog \[ X=\bigvee_{n\ge1}[0,1/n],\qquad Y=\{0\}, \] with the metric \(|s-t|\) on one arm and \(s+t\) on distinct arms. It is compact metric. The radial contraction \(h((n,s),t)=(n,(1-t)s)\) makes \(Y\) tame, strictly off \(Y\) until the final time; the holink map to a point is a fibration. Thus the two-step filtration is homotopically stratified in Quinn's general definition. It has no mapping-cylinder neighborhood of \(Y\). Every neighborhood contains all sufficiently short arms, including their terminal endpoints, and these endpoints converge to \(Y\). In a mapping-cylinder neighborhood with radial coordinate \(r\), a point with \(0<r<1\) lies on an embedded interval through itself, obtained by varying \(r\) in both directions. A terminal endpoint of an arm cannot be an interior point of any embedded interval in \(X\). Hence every such endpoint would have to lie on the outer level \(r=1\). Continuity is contradicted by their convergence to the apex \(r=0\). The same argument applies after making the cylinder smaller. Therefore \(\Sigma_d\) in the actual collar/mapping-cylinder sense need not exist for a general HSS. Equations (51), (56), (57), (69), the holink comparison, and the finite spectral sequence have the independent pro-homotopy proofs above. An equality \(V_d\simeq\Sigma_d\) requires an actual compatible conical deployment, or must define a replacement \(\Sigma_d\) using the full iterated holink diagram. The example uses Quinn's general strata, not manifold strata; no claim is made here that it satisfies an additional manifold-strata hypothesis.

statement: Canonical homotopy-class sector comparison for filtered normal-crossings bundles, including rank0/empty cases, branch permutations and orbifold stabilizers.
source_statement_latex: \label{c4.06-proved-the-canonical-normal-crossings-comparison} The notation here is checked in the original scans 147/173--177 \cite{C_Grothendieck147}. Their notation is a filtered normal bundle over \(B=D_{d_*}^*\), with a pair \(d_0''\le d_0'\) of entries of the flag and an exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow A=\check N_{d_*,d_0'} \longrightarrow E=\check N_{d_*,d_0''} \xrightarrow{q}Q=\check N_{d_*,(d_0',d_0'')} \longrightarrow0. \] This is (286)--(287). The normal-crossings branches give \(Q\) a local decomposition into complex lines, with transitions allowed to permute those lines. Write \(Q^*\) for the complement of all coordinate hyperplanes. Thus its fibre is \((\mathbb C^*)^r\), not \(\mathbb C^r\setminus\{0\}\). For rank zero, the empty coordinate arrangement has complement the whole zero bundle; the torus fibre is a point. The same argument then applies without a puncture, and an empty base gives the empty equivalence. Page175(290) defines \(E^*=q^{-1}(Q^*)\); (291) describes \(E^*\to Q^*\) as a torsor for the pulled-back additive bundle \(A\). The quotient map \(q:E^*\to Q^*\) is a canonical homotopy equivalence. Choose a Hermitian splitting \(E=A\oplus Q\); then \((a,v)\mapsto((1-t)a,v)\) contracts the kernel and proves the claim. Splittings form an affine space, so their homotopies identify all inverse choices. The map \(q\) itself does not depend on a splitting. The sector tube \(V^{d_0'}_{d_*,d_0''}\) is, by definition of the normal-crossings incidence sector, the neighborhood germ of \(B\) in the \(E\)-directions, with precisely the coordinates belonging to \(Q\) required to be nonzero. Its pro-homotopy type has a canonical comparison with \(E^*\). Here is a construction and a check of its ambiguity. For a simple normal crossings divisor, use its divisor line bundles with defining sections. Choose an ordinary smooth tubular projection onto the intersection \(B\) and connections on those line bundles. Parallel transport identifies their restrictions on a small neighborhood with their pullbacks from \(B\); the tuple of defining sections then has differential the normal-coordinate isomorphism along \(B\). The inverse function theorem, after variable-radius shrinking, gives an adapted tubular germ from the direct sum of the normal lines to the original space. It takes every coordinate hyperplane and every flag subbundle to the corresponding divisor incidence. This constructs the required sector comparison. Normalize each adapted tubular germ to have identity derivative on the intrinsic normal bundle, by composing with the inverse of its fibrewise normal derivative. This preserves the coordinate arrangement and the flag subbundles. Arbitrary normal-bundle automorphisms are not being declared homotopic to the identity. If a kernel block has no chosen line decomposition, retain its coordinates from an ordinary tubular chart and use the defining sections in the quotient block; the same inverse-function argument respects every flag subbundle. If \(\Phi,\Psi\) are two adapted tubular germs with the same normal derivative, their transition \(g=\Psi^{-1}\Phi\) fixes the zero section and has identity normal derivative. Fibre dilations give \[ g_t=\delta_{1/t}\,g\,\delta_t\quad(t>0),\qquad g_0=\mathrm{id}. \] Taylor's formula in normal coordinates shows this is a continuous, indeed smooth, family of germs through \(t=0\); its tangential displacement tends to zero and its normal derivative tends to the identity. Every \(g_t\) preserves the coordinate-hyperplane arrangement. Restricting to sufficiently small variable-radius neighborhoods makes the family defined for all \(t\in[0,1]\). The same construction works for parameter families. Hence the induced comparison on the sector has a unique homotopy class, compatible with refinements and changes of tubular choices. This supplies the canonical meaning that the manuscript explicitly leaves unresolved below (294). The small-sector pro-germ also compares explicitly with the entire punctured bundle. For a bundle norm and a positive continuous radius function \(\eta\) on the base, the inclusion \(\{v\in E^*:\|v\|<\eta(\pi v)\}\hookrightarrow E^*\) is a homotopy equivalence. An inverse up to homotopy is \[ v\longmapsto \frac{\eta(\pi v)}{\eta(\pi v)+\|v\|}v. \] Interpolation of its strictly positive scalar factor with \(1\) supplies both inverse homotopies and preserves every coordinate nonvanishing condition. Such variable-radius disk neighborhoods are cofinal by the tubular chart and paracompactness of the base. Their natural inclusions therefore identify the sector prospace with the constant space \(E^*\), coherently under shrinking. Combining it with \(q\) gives the precise statement \[ V^{d_0'}_{d_*,d_0''} \ \simeq\ \left.\check N_{d_*,(d_0',d_0'')}^{\,*}\right|_{D_{d_*}^*}. \] The ambiguity is homotopy, not a distinguished homeomorphism of neighborhoods. A Hermitian norm further retracts each punctured line to its unit-circle bundle, giving the corresponding torus bundle; metrics form a convex space of choices. For normal crossings with branch monodromy, perform the construction on the finite local branch-label cover. The normal line bundles and the quotient map descend equivariantly, as does the homotopy-class comparison, because the coordinate arrangement and the dilation are invariant under branch permutations. On a Deligne--Mumford orbifold chart finite-group averaging supplies invariant auxiliary metrics and connections. Thus the result is canonical in the incidence/orbifold category. Passing to an unlabelled orbit-poset and discarding stabilizers would lose data.

statement: Bare order/face identities do not force product-collar transversality in TOP/PL/smooth; even proper smooth Hurewicz maps can fail smooth normal-product regularity.
source_statement_latex: \label{c5.02-refuted-in-all-three-categories-automatic-transversality} Use \(I=\{0<1<2\}\), \[ \Sigma_0=\{*\},\quad \Sigma_1=\mathbb R\times[0,\infty),\quad \Sigma_2=\mathbb R\times[0,\infty)^2. \] Write \((x,t,r)\) on the last space and take \[ \Sigma_{01}=\mathbb R\times\{0\},\quad \Sigma_{12}=\{r=0\},\quad \Sigma_{02}=\{t=0\}. \] All targets are face inclusions and \(s_{01},s_{02}\) are constant. Put \[ s_{12}(x,t,0)=(xt,t) \] for the smooth example. For a PL example replace \(xt\) by \(f(x,t)=\max(-t,\min(x,t))\), a finite piecewise-linear function. The incoming faces are closed, properly embedded, and transversely collared. Their intersection is \(\{t=r=0\}=s_{12}^{-1}\Sigma_{01}\), and projection control holds because both maps to \(\Sigma_0\) are constant. Thus the induced relation is a topological order with finite totally ordered lower intervals; every bare algebraic and face condition in the proposed implication holds. The source is not assumed fibrant in the general Scholium or its /062 margin. Yet \(s_{12}\) is not transverse to the base boundary in the collar-product meaning explicitly used at /025--027 and /031. Its boundary restriction maps the whole \(x\)-axis to \((0,0)\). If a collar-product description existed near that axis, the image of a small collar neighborhood would lie in a one-dimensional collar through that point. In either example the image of every sufficiently small neighborhood of \((0,0)\) contains a nonempty open two-dimensional wedge: in the smooth example \(|u|<\delta t\), and in the PL example \(|u|<t\). A one-dimensional embedded collar cannot contain an open subset of a two-dimensional manifold, by invariance of dimension. Thus the specified collar-product transversality fails even topologically. This terminology must be retained: the smooth map does satisfy ordinary differential transversality to the target boundary, which is a weaker requirement here. A sufficient extra hypothesis is local triviality of the entire boundary diagram over the base collar, with its trivializations preserving all its faces. Pulling that diagram back along the collar's product coordinate then gives compatible product collars. This is the strong equisingularity qualification in /039; an unspecified use of ``fibrant'' must not be substituted for it. Even adding raw proper Hurewicz fibrancy does not imply the smooth product-collar condition. Take \(\Sigma_0=\{*\}\), \(\Sigma_1=[0,1]\), \(\Sigma_2=[0,1]^2\), \(\Sigma_{01}=\{0,1\}\), \(\Sigma_{12}=[0,1]\times\{0,1\}\), and \(\Sigma_{02}=\{0,1\}\times[0,1]\). Let \(s_{12}(u,v)=u^2\) and let the other sources be constant. Every source is proper and Hurewicz: on each component \(u\mapsto u^2\) is a homeomorphism. All target collars, intersections, and projection-control identities hold. But the derivative of \(s_{12}\) in the normal direction at \(u=0\) is zero, invariant under smooth collar changes; a smooth product over that collar has nonzero normal derivative. Thus the smooth source transversality fails. statement: Proper locally trivial TOP source bundle with manifold objects and whole-boundary target can have a nonmanifold fiber.
source_statement_latex: \label{c5.03-refuted-in-top-automatic-manifold-fibres} Let \(H\) be the Poincare homology three-sphere and \(F=\Sigma H\) its suspension. Then \(F\) is a compact polyhedron which is not a topological manifold: near either suspension vertex the punctured neighborhood is \(H\times(0,\epsilon)\), whose nontrivial fundamental group cannot become that of a punctured four-ball. More precisely the nested punctured cone neighborhoods all induce isomorphisms on that nontrivial group, whereas a four-manifold has a basis of punctured simply-connected ball neighborhoods. Cannon's double-suspension theorem gives \(\Sigma^2H\cong S^5\). Removing the two outer suspension points gives \(F\times\mathbb R\cong S^4\times\mathbb R\): the image of those two points can be sent to the north and south poles by a homeomorphism of \(S^5\). Consequently \(E=F\times S^1\) is a closed topological five-manifold, since it is locally \(F\times\mathbb R\). Take \(\Sigma_0=S^1,\ \Sigma_1=E\times[0,1]\), with incoming face \(\Sigma_{01}=E\times\{0,1\}=\partial\Sigma_1\), and source projection to \(S^1\). This is a proper locally trivial topological bundle, with fibre \(F\amalg F\). Both object spaces are manifolds and the target is the whole boundary. All triple, order, and transversality conditions are vacuous. The fibre is not a manifold. This disproves the mixed-fibre implication at /051 and /063 even with genuine bundles, not merely homotopy fibrations. The precise primary statements used here are Cannon \cite[Theorem 1.5, p.833; Corollary 3.6, p.838]{C_Cannon}.

statement: A transverse product-collared incidence system built from the suspension of a homology sphere has manifold object spaces and proper bundle sources but nonmanifold incoming faces, refuting the corresponding automatic TOP face assertions.
source_statement_latex: \label{c5.04-refuted-in-top-automatic-manifold-faces} Use the same compact polyhedron \(F=\Sigma H\) as in C5.03, and put \[ \Sigma_0=\{*\},\qquad \Sigma_1=[0,1],\qquad \Sigma_2=F\times[0,1]^2. \] Let \(\Sigma_{01}=\{0,1\}\), \(\Sigma_{12}=F\times[0,1]\times\{0,1\}\), and \(\Sigma_{02}=F\times\{0,1\}\times[0,1]\). In coordinates \((z,u,v)\), the source \(s_{12}\) is projection to \(u\), and \(s_{01},s_{02}\) are constant to the point. The square is locally a plane at its interior points and a half-plane at every boundary point, including its vertices. Since \(F\times\mathbb R\) is a five-manifold by C5.03, \(\Sigma_2\) is a compact topological six-manifold with boundary. Its whole boundary is \(F\times\partial([0,1]^2)\cong F\times S^1\), itself a five-manifold. It is the union of the two specified collective faces. These faces have their evident transverse product collars, and \[ \Sigma_{12}\cap\Sigma_{02} =F\times\{0,1\}^2=s_{12}^{-1}(\Sigma_{01}). \] The source \(s_{12}\) respects the base collars, and projection control holds because the other two source maps are constant. Every object \(\Sigma_i\) is a manifold with boundary. All source maps are now proper Hurewicz fibrations: \(s_{12}\) is a product bundle with compact fibre \(F\amalg F\), and the other targets are points. Thus even adding equisingularity does not repair this TOP face assertion. Each incoming face is a disjoint union of two copies of \(F\times[0,1]\), which is not a manifold with boundary. At positive interior interval coordinates the space is a five-manifold. At an endpoint its local homology vanishes in all degrees, since the relative local homology of the half-interval factor vanishes. Hence, if the product were a five-manifold with boundary, its intrinsic boundary would be exactly \(F\times\{0,1\}\). The boundary of a manifold with boundary is a manifold, contradicting the proved singularity of \(F\). The full family therefore satisfies the surrounding order, properness, source-fibrancy, target-collar and source-transversality conditions while its incoming faces are not manifolds. This refutes both the /067 margin and the version of /051(d) that tries to deduce manifold flag spaces from c) and the object-manifold part of d).

statement: Precise positive PL bundle and smooth source-system fiber/face/boundary conclusions, including vertical-face regularity from the full control system and all boundary formulas.
source_statement_latex: \label{c5.05-proved-for-pl-bundles-and-smooth-submersions} Work with the entire completed incidence system of C2.02, its transverse target collars, and its full boundary decomposition. Impose the following regularity on every source map. The positive PL and smooth assertions require these category-specific meanings of fibrancy. In PL assume the source is a locally trivial PL bundle and every collar and transition is PL. In the smooth case assume every source is a proper smooth submersion with the stated product behavior on horizontal faces. Together with full projection control this gives the vertical-face regularity proved below; alternatively one may start with the corresponding smooth bundles of corner manifolds. A map which is merely smooth and a Hurewicz fibration need not have the required differential regularity. First, in PL, a locally finite polyhedron \(F\) such that \(F\times\mathbb R^m\) is a PL manifold is itself a PL manifold. Use a product triangulation and choose a top-dimensional simplex in the second factor. The link of its interior product with a vertex of \(F\) is the link of that vertex in \(F\). In a PL manifold that link is a PL sphere or ball, according as the point is interior or boundary. The link criterion gives the conclusion, at every vertex and then throughout \(F\). Applying this in a local bundle trivialization over an interior base point proves that the fibre is a PL manifold with boundary/corners; local triviality identifies the other fibres with it. In the smooth case first verify tangential surjectivity on every vertical face, using the whole source-map system. On \(\Sigma_{ikj}\), with \(i<k<j\), projection control gives \[ s_{ij}|_{\Sigma_{ikj}} =s_{ik}\circ(s_{kj}|_{\Sigma_{ikj}}). \] The horizontal pullback and product-collar condition makes \(s_{kj}|_{\Sigma_{ikj}}:\Sigma_{ikj}\to\Sigma_{ik}\) a submersion, while \(s_{ik}\) is another source submersion. Thus one can choose horizontal lifts tangent to all those faces; in a product corner chart take such lifts simultaneously and combine them with a partition of unity. Horizontal base-boundary coordinates are separated by the specified product collars. The corner submersion theorem now gives fibre charts by fixing the base coordinates, so the fibre is a manifold with corners. Properness allows these lifts to be integrated over a common base neighbourhood, giving compatible local trivializations. An isolated smooth submersion lacking these vertical-face checks would not justify that conclusion. In both categories a local chart on an arrow space \(\Sigma_{ij}\) therefore separates into base coordinates, horizontal base-boundary coordinates, fibre coordinates, and vertical fibre-boundary coordinates. The horizontal faces are exactly \(\Sigma_{kij}\), \(k<i\), by the inverse-image identity; the vertical faces are exactly \(\Sigma_{ikj}\), \(i<k<j\), by the full boundary decomposition and the ordering of the incoming labels. Thus \[ \partial\Sigma_{ij} =\bigcup_{k<i}\Sigma_{kij} \ \cup\! \bigcup_{i<k<j}\Sigma_{ikj}, \] while the intrinsic boundary of each source fibre consists only of the latter, intermediate-index pieces. These formulas include all corners through their intersections. This proves the mixed-fibre and face-boundary conclusions of /051, /063, and /067 under these precise PL and smooth hypotheses. For /067 alone, no source bundle is needed if the incoming collars and all ambient spaces are PL/smooth: the same local link criterion in PL, or the smooth collar chart in the smooth category, proves that each transverse face intersection is a manifold with corners. statement: Compact finite-dimensional connected TOP counterexample satisfies raw source fibrancy, proper local target embedding, collared endpoint and source transversality but has an internal strict arrow; open-source correction.
source_statement_latex: \label{c5.07-refuted-in-top-connected-components-suffice} The word ``connected'' in /068--071 cannot be replaced silently by ``path-connected.'' Even all the stated finiteness, properness, local-immersion, and collared-target conditions permit a strict arrow within one connected component. The following example also satisfies the stronger bordant-target condition of /063, not just the nowhere-dense condition of /069. Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^2\) be a compact, nondegenerate hereditarily indecomposable continuum, for example the plane pseudoarc constructed by R. H. Bing, \emph{Concerning hereditarily indecomposable continua}, Example 1, printed pp.43--44 \cite{C_Bing1951}. Every path in \(K\) is constant. Indeed, a nonconstant path has a nondegenerate image continuum. Uniform continuity partitions its domain into finitely many consecutive intervals whose image continua all have diameter smaller than that whole image. The image would then be a finite union of proper continua with connected successive unions. Indecomposability rules this out, by induction on the number of pieces. Choose a continuous map \(q:[1,\infty)\to\mathbb R^2\) whose cluster set at infinity is exactly \(K\), with \(\operatorname{dist}(q(t),K)\to0\). Here is an explicit existence construction. Fix a point of \(K\). For each positive integer \(n\), choose a finite \(1/n\)-net in \(K\). Its open \(1/n\)-neighbourhood in the plane is connected and hence path-connected. On \([n,n+1]\), let \(q\) traverse a piecewise linear loop, based at the fixed point, which visits every point of that net and stays in that neighbourhood. Concatenation is continuous. These visits show that every point of \(K\) is a cluster point; the neighbourhood bound excludes any other cluster point. Set \[ C=\{(q(t),1/t):t\ge1\}\subset\mathbb R^3, \qquad P=C\cup(K\times\{0\}). \] The height coordinate identifies \(C\) with the ray \([1,\infty)\). The space \(P\) is its compact closure, hence is a connected compact metric space of finite covering dimension at most three. The dimension bound can be checked directly: for any finite open cover of this compact subset of \(\mathbb R^3\), choose a sufficiently fine triangulation of \(\mathbb R^3\). Its vertex open-star cover restricts to a refinement on \(P\), by the Lebesgue number of the given cover; each point lies in at most four such stars, the vertices of its carrier simplex. This is the defining covering-dimension bound. Its single connected component is open. Write \(b=(q(1),1)\); its neighbourhood with height greater than \(1/(1+\epsilon)\) is a collar \([0,\epsilon)\) of the point \(b\). Choose \(a\in K\times\{0\}\). The path component of \(a\) in \(P\) is the singleton \(\{a\}\). To verify this, suppose a path starting in the remainder enters \(C\). An interval component of the inverse image of \(C\) has a finite left endpoint at which the height is zero. On that interval the corresponding ray parameter tends to infinity at its left endpoint. By the intermediate value theorem, the image of every sufficiently short interval after that endpoint contains an entire tail \([T,\infty)\) of ray parameters. Continuity of the path would therefore force the whole tail of \(q\) to converge to the same remainder point. This contradicts its nondegenerate cluster set \(K\). A path remaining in the remainder is constant by the preceding indecomposability argument. Give \(P\) the order with relation \[ R=\Delta_P\cup\{(a,b)\}\subset P\times P. \] This is a closed partial order. Its strict relation consists of one point, which is a clopen component of \(R\); the other component is \(\Delta_P\cong P\). Every lower interval is totally ordered and has at most two elements. Both projections \(s,b:R\to P\) are proper because the domain is compact. The target projection is a local embedding: it is the identity on the diagonal component and the embedding of a point on the strict component. The strict target image \(\{b\}\) is nowhere dense and collared. Thus its family of incoming boundary germs is transverse; there is at most one such germ at any point. The source projection is a Hurewicz fibration, including its full lifting property for arbitrary parameter spaces. Given a map \(g:Z\to R\) and a homotopy \(H:Z\times[0,1]\to P\) with \(H(z,0)=s(g(z))\), let \(Z_e\) be the inverse image of the isolated strict arrow. This is clopen in \(Z\). On \(Z_e\), each path \(H(z,-)\) starts at \(a\), so it is constant; lift it constantly to the strict arrow. On \(Z\setminus Z_e\), lift by \((H(z,t),H(z,t))\in\Delta_P\). These continuous lifts agree with the initial map and glue across the clopen partition. Source transversality to the target collar is also satisfied: on the identity component it is the identity, while the strict component maps to \(a\), outside a chosen collar of \(b\). Nevertheless \(a<b\) lie in the same connected component of \(P\). The map to the one-point set of connected components is not strictly increasing. This refutes the unrestricted TOP conclusion of /070 and therefore the equivalence claimed in /071 in that scope. The additional monomorphism condition for distinct components is vacuous here and cannot repair it. No doubtful transcription is used: the original /070--071 explicitly says connected components, as does the open-component assumption on /068. The exact correction proved in C5.01 is to use open, path-connected components; in particular it applies to manifolds and locally path-connected PL spaces. Another sufficient correction, which can use connected components without local path-connectedness, is to require the proper source map to be open. Here is the additional proof. Suppose a strict arrow has source and target in the same open connected component \(D\). The strict arrows whose targets lie in \(D\) form a clopen subspace of \(R\). Their source image is open by openness of \(s\), and closed by properness; it meets \(D\), so it contains all of \(D\). Thus every point of \(D\) has a strict successor in \(D\). Starting at one point gives arbitrarily long strict chains in its compact upper interval. Proper local injectivity of the target projection makes the cardinalities of lower intervals locally bounded, hence bounded on that compact upper interval, a contradiction. The same open-and-closed image argument aligns middle objects to prove transitivity of the component relation. Cycles would give a strict chain returning to a component and then the same contradiction. Total ordering of the pointwise lower intervals gives the proper-injective target comparison of C5.01. A locally trivial source bundle is open, so this correction applies to the strong equisingular interpretation too.

Let a topological category have Hausdorff object and arrow spaces, open manifold components of its object space, proper locally embedding target map \(b\), Hurewicz source map \(s\), and locally nowhere-dense target image of the strict arrows. Here is a full proof which avoids the manuscript's dimension inequalities. The identity section is closed by Hausdorffness and open by local injectivity of \(b\): near an identity, both that section and a sufficiently small arrow neighbourhood lie in a target-injective chart, so the only arrow in that chart with a given nearby target is its identity. Hence strict arrows form a clopen subspace. Source lifting along a path cannot change from a strict arrow to an identity, and target continuity keeps its target in one component. It follows that the existence of an arrow from one component to another is independent of which source point in the first component is prescribed. Suppose a strict arrow has source and target in the same connected \(n\)-manifold component \(D\), allowing boundary or corners. Invariance of domain makes the image of \(b\sigma\) open in \(\mathbb R^n\); it cannot meet the boundary of that orthant, and hence is open in \(D\). This contradicts the locally nowhere-dense strict target image. Thus no strict arrow has both endpoints in one component. statement: Canonical infinity-categorical collage pushout across a minimal groupoidal label for a complete Segal object conservative over a finite poset.
source_statement_latex: Let $P$ be a finite poset and let $\mathcal C_\bullet$ be a complete Segal object in spaces, conservative over $N(P)$. Let $i\in P$ be minimal, let $A=\mathcal C_i$ (an $\infty$-groupoid), and let $\mathcal D=\mathcal C|_{P\setminus\{i\}}$. Let $\mathcal M$ be the category of arrows of $\mathcal C$ whose source is in $A$ and whose target is in $\mathcal D$. Morphisms in $\mathcal M$ are commutative squares, with the source-side arrow necessarily an equivalence. Write $q:\mathcal M\to A$ and $p:\mathcal M\to\mathcal D$ for the source and target functors. Then there is a canonical pushout formula in $\operatorname{Cat}_\infty$ \[ \mathcal C\simeq A\mathbin{\coprod}_{\mathcal M\times\{0\}} (\mathcal M\times[1]) \mathbin{\coprod}_{\mathcal M\times\{1\}}\mathcal D. \tag{C1.B1} \] The maps from the two endpoints are $q$ and $p$, respectively. The comparison is induced by the tautological natural transformation from the source to the target of an arrow.

statement: Crossing-arrow category of the controlled fibrant deployment is the actual category M, with target a left fibration and source defined by projection control.
source_statement_latex: Suppose the deployment is a finite graded topological category with object spaces $\Sigma_j$, arrow spaces $\Sigma_{jk}$ for $j<k$, and identities only within each object space. Suppose its source maps $s_{jk}:\Sigma_{jk}\to\Sigma_j$ are fibrations and the flag identities and control equations are \[ \Sigma_{ijk}=s_{jk}^{-1}(\Sigma_{ij})\subset\Sigma_{jk}, \qquad s_{ik}=s_{ij}s_{jk}\quad\hbox{on }\Sigma_{ijk}. \tag{C1.B3} \] Here $\Sigma_{ij}\hookrightarrow\Sigma_j$ is the target inclusion, and $s_{jk}$ in the second equation is restricted to $\Sigma_{ijk}\to\Sigma_{ij}$. Define a topological category $M_i$ with objects $\coprod_{j>i}\Sigma_{ij}$, arrows $\coprod_{i<j<k}\Sigma_{ijk}$, and the induced source, target and composition maps. Then, after passing to complete Segal objects, $M_i$ is the $\mathcal M$ of C1.B1. Its target functor $p:M_i\to\mathcal D$ is a left fibration. Its source functor $q:M_i\to\Sigma_i$ is well defined by the control equation.

statement: Simultaneous inward pushes after deleting a lower ideal preserve remaining strata and commute with the stated source/face maps, hence give exit equivalences.

It restricts to a homotopy of $Z^\circ_R$. Therefore $Z^\circ_R\hookrightarrow Z$ induces an equivalence on exit categories when the retained outer faces are ignored as separate strata.
